title: How a computer runs a program
summary: Follow one C program from source text to a running process: compiling and linking, bits and hex, the fetch-decode-execute loop, branches, the stack, caches, pipelines, system calls and virtual memory.
outcomes: Explain what the preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker and OS loader each do, and how static and dynamic linking differ
Convert between binary, hex and decimal, and read two's complement and little-endian bytes
Trace x86-64 assembly instruction by instruction, tracking registers and the program counter
Explain how cmp sets the flags and why signed and unsigned comparisons use different jumps
Explain how call, ret and the stack pointer implement function calls, and why returning a pointer to a local is a bug
Compute average memory access time and predict which loop order is cache friendly
Explain how pipelining and branch prediction speed up code and why mispredicted branches are slow
Explain how system calls, timer interrupts and page tables let the OS protect and share the machine

lessons.title: From hello.c to a running process

blocks.md: A CPU cannot read C. It only executes **machine code**: instructions encoded as bytes, sitting in memory. Running `./hello` therefore needs two separate jobs. First a **toolchain** translates your source text into an executable file of machine code. Later the **operating system** (OS) turns that file into a running **process**: the program while it runs, with its own memory and state that the OS keeps track of. This lesson walks the whole path once; the rest of the course zooms into each stage.

blocks.caption: The four stages GCC documents: preprocessing, compilation proper, assembly and linking, always in that order. Plain `gcc hello.c -o hello` runs all four.

blocks.md:
Each stage has one job:

- **Preprocessor**: pastes in `#include` files and expands macros. Output is still C text.
- **Compiler**: translates C into **assembly**, a human-readable text form of machine instructions for one CPU family (for example x86-64, the 64-bit version of the instruction family that began with Intel's 8086 chip and runs most PCs and servers).
- **Assembler**: encodes each assembly instruction as bytes, producing an **object file** (`.o`).
- **Linker**: combines object files and libraries into one **executable**, filling in the addresses of functions defined elsewhere. Each named function or global variable in an object file is a **symbol**; a call to a symbol defined in another file stays undefined until the linker fills in its address.

The last step belongs to the OS. Its core, the **kernel**, is the part that runs with full control of the hardware. The shell starts a program in two steps, both requests to the kernel (lesson 8 shows how such requests work). **fork** makes a copy of the shell process; the copy then calls **execve**, which replaces its program with hello, so the shell itself keeps running and waits for hello to finish. The kernel gives the program fresh memory regions (stack, heap and data, mapped out in lesson 5) and starts it at its **entry point**, the address of its first instruction.

blocks.title: The path from source text to a process

scenes.caption: Everything starts as text you wrote. Nothing here can run yet.
The preprocessor expands #include and macros. The compiler then turns C into assembly for one CPU family, here x86-64.
The assembler encodes instructions as bytes. hello.o holds real machine code for main, but its library call (GCC turned this printf into puts) points at a symbol that is still undefined.

The linker combines hello.o with startup code, checks that the C library provides puts, and writes an ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) executable: a file describing which bytes to place where in memory.

When you type ./hello, the shell forks a copy of itself and the copy calls execve. The kernel replaces that copy's program with hello: new stack, heap and data segments, then jumps to its entry point.

By default puts is not copied in: hello only records that it needs libc.so.6. At start-up the dynamic linker, ld-linux, maps the C library into the process and arranges for the address of puts to be filled in, by default the first time it is called.

blocks.prompt: `hello.o` already contains machine code for `main`. Why can't the OS run `hello.o` directly?
blocks.reveal: Because it is incomplete. Build it with `gcc` and run `objdump -t hello.o`: the call's target is listed as `*UND*` (undefined). It is named `puts`, not `printf`: GCC quietly replaces `printf` of a constant string ending in a newline with the cheaper `puts`, even at -O0 (optimization level zero, meaning no optimization). `objdump -r` shows a **relocation**: a note saying "patch the address of puts into these bytes later". Only the linker knows where `puts` will end up, so only the linked executable is runnable.

blocks.md: The executable on Linux uses the **ELF** format (described in `man 5 elf`, section 5 of the Unix manual pages, which covers file formats). Besides the machine code (the `.text` section) and initialized global data (`.data`), it carries a **program header table** that tells the OS which parts of the file to map into memory, at which addresses, with which permissions. If the program uses **shared libraries** (libraries loaded at run time and shared by many programs, like the C library), ELF also names an **interpreter** (the dynamic loader; for glibc, the GNU C library, usually `ld-linux`) that execve uses to load those libraries.

**Static or dynamic linking.** A library can join the program in two ways. With **static linking** (`gcc -static`) the linker copies the library code the program uses into the executable. With **dynamic linking**, the default for the C library on Linux, the linker only records which **shared libraries** the executable needs (`libc.so.6` for hello) and leaves calls such as `puts` unresolved. When execve starts the program, it first runs the interpreter named in the ELF file, the **dynamic linker** `ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`, which finds the libraries, maps them into the process and fills in their addresses. By default it looks each function up only the first time it is called (the `ld.so(8)` man page documents `LD_BIND_NOW` to do it all at start-up instead).

blocks.caption: The program lists the shared libraries the kernel and ld-linux mapped into its own address space (from /proc/self/maps, a file Linux provides for each process). Real output from two builds of the same source on Compiler Explorer, a website that compiles and runs code; sizes vary by toolchain.

blocks.md: The numbers show the trade-off. The static build is 60 times larger because it carries its own copy of every C library function it uses, and Carnegie Mellon University's (CMU) systems course, 15-213, lists the costs: duplicated code in every executable and in memory, and a bug fix in a system library means relinking every program. A shared library is stored once, shared by all the processes that use it, and fixed in one place. The price is a dependency: a dynamically linked program starts only if a compatible library is installed on the machine, and every start does the extra work of loading and linking it. The `ldd` command lists the shared libraries a program needs.

Loading is not copying the whole file up front. As *Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces* (OSTEP) explains, modern OSes load lazily: they set up the mapping and bring in pieces of code or data only when they are first touched. The OS also creates the **stack**, puts `argc` and `argv` on it for `main`, sets up the standard input, output and error file descriptors, and finally transfers control to the program. A **file descriptor** is a small integer the OS hands a process to name an open file or device; by convention 0 is standard input, 1 standard output and 2 standard error.

A **program** is a file of bytes on disk. A **process** is a running instance of it: its own memory (code, data, heap, stack), its own register values (the CPU's working slots, lesson 3), and OS bookkeeping such as open files. One program can be running as many processes at once.

Misconception: "the compiler makes something the CPU runs straight off the disk." The CPU only fetches instructions from memory. An executable is inert until the OS loader maps it into a process's memory and points the CPU at its entry point.

blocks.question: You split a program into `main.c` and `util.c`. `main.c` calls `parse()` defined in `util.c`. Which stage is the first one that needs to see both files?
options: The preprocessor, because it must find parse()
The compiler, because it must check parse() exists
The assembler, because it encodes the call instruction
The linker, because it resolves the call to parse() across object files
blocks.explain: Each .c file is preprocessed, compiled and assembled on its own; a declaration of `parse` (usually from a header) is enough for the compiler. The call is left as an undefined symbol plus a relocation in main.o. The linker is the first stage that sees both object files and patches the real address in.

blocks.question: Which statement about running `./hello` is correct?
options: The shell reads hello's machine code and executes it itself
The CPU loads the ELF file from disk one instruction at a time as it runs
The kernel, via execve, replaces the current process image with hello and starts it at its entry point
The linker runs again every time you start the program
blocks.explain: execve(2): the program currently run by the calling process is replaced with a new one, with a newly initialized stack, heap and data segments. The CPU never reads from the disk file directly; pages of the file are mapped into memory and loaded when touched.

lessons.title: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored

blocks.md: Every value the CPU touches, an instruction, an address, a character or a number, is stored as **bits**. A bit is one binary digit, 0 or 1; Claude Shannon's 1948 paper on information theory introduced the word as short for *binary digit*, crediting the statistician John Tukey with it. Take the number 42. In everyday decimal its digits weigh 10 and 1: 4 x 10 + 2. In binary each digit weighs a power of two, so 42 is `00101010`: 32 + 8 + 2. The next lessons read addresses like `0x1000` and bytes like `f4`; this lesson explains that notation and the few encodings the rest of the course relies on.

scenes.caption: Eight bits, each worth twice the one to its right. All zeros is 0. To write 42, take the largest place values that fit, left to right.
32 is the largest place value that fits in 42, so its bit is 1. That leaves 10.
8 fits in 10, leaving 2, and the 2s bit finishes it: 32 + 8 + 2 = 42, written 00101010 in binary.
Split the byte into two halves of 4 bits. 0010 is 2 and 1010 is 8 + 2 = 10, written a. So 42 is 0x2a in hex.

blocks.md: Long binary strings are hard to read, so programmers write them in **hexadecimal** (hex), base 16. Its digits are 0 to 9 and then a to f for 10 to 15, and the prefix `0x` marks a hex number in C and in assembly listings. One hex digit covers exactly 4 bits ($2^4 = 16$), so converting is mechanical: replace each hex digit with its 4 bits, or the other way round. `0x2a` is 0010 1010, which is $2 \times 16 + 10 = 42$. Place values in hex are powers of 16, so `0x1000` is $16^3 = 4096$ and `0x1008` is 0x1000 + 8 = 4104.

A **byte** is 8 bits: two hex digits, `0x00` to `0xff`. Memory is addressed in bytes: each address names one byte, and a larger value occupies several consecutive addresses. A **word** is the natural size the CPU computes with; on x86-64 that is 64 bits, so registers, `long` and pointers are 8 bytes (an `int` stays 4). That is why addresses are 64-bit numbers and why consecutive `long`s sit 8 addresses apart. (Intel's assembly names keep the old 16-bit meaning of word, so lesson 3 calls a 64-bit value a quadword.)

n bits have $2^n$ patterns, so read as **unsigned** numbers (never negative) they cover 0 to $2^n - 1$: 0 to 255 for a byte, 0 to about $1.8 \times 10^{19}$ for 64 bits.

Arithmetic on n bits keeps only the low n bits of the result. In a byte, 255 + 1 is 256 = 1 0000 0000, which needs 9 bits; the carry out of the top bit is dropped and the byte holds 0. C defines unsigned arithmetic exactly this way, as arithmetic modulo $2^n$.

Negative numbers use **two's complement**, the encoding x86-64 uses and, since C23, the only one the C standard allows. The rule: the top bit's weight is negative. In a byte the weights are -128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, so a signed byte ranges from -128 (1000 0000) to 127 (0111 1111). Take -12: start at -128 and add 116 = 64 + 32 + 16 + 4. That gives 1111 0100, which is `0xf4`.

scenes.caption: 0111 1111. With the top bit clear, both readings agree: 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 127, the largest signed byte.
Add 1. The bits become 1000 0000. Unsigned, that is 128. In two's complement the top bit weighs -128, so the very same byte reads -128.
0xf4 = 1111 0100: 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 4 = 244 unsigned, or -128 + 116 = -12 signed. With the top bit set, the signed reading is always the unsigned one minus 256.
All ones: 255 unsigned, -1 signed.
Add 1 again. The carry falls off the top and the byte is 0. The same adder gave the right answer for both readings: 255 + 1 wraps to 0, and -1 + 1 is 0.

blocks.md:
To negate a two's complement number, invert every bit and add 1. 12 is 0000 1100; inverted, 1111 0011; plus 1, 1111 0100 = `0xf4` = -12. Addition is the same bit operation for signed and unsigned numbers, so one adder circuit serves both; only the reading of the result differs.

Widening a signed value to more bits uses **sign extension**: copy the top bit into every new bit. -12 as a byte is `0xf4`; as a 32-bit `int` it is `0xfffffff4`, still -12. An unsigned value is widened with zeros instead: `0xf4` becomes `0x000000f4`, 244.

blocks.prompt: A byte holds `1000 0000`. A program prints it once as an unsigned number and once as a signed one. What two values appear, and which one does the CPU consider correct?
blocks.reveal: **128** and **-128**, and the CPU has no opinion. Registers and memory hold bare bits with no type attached; the instruction that uses them decides the meaning. An unsigned compare or widening reads the byte as 128, a signed one as -128. Lesson 4 shows that x86-64 has separate conditional jumps for exactly this reason.

blocks.md: A value wider than a byte occupies several addresses, so the CPU needs an order. x86-64 is **little-endian**: the least significant byte goes at the lowest address. The 4-byte `int` 42, `0x0000002a`, sits in memory as `2a 00 00 00`. **Big-endian** machines and network protocols use the opposite order, `00 00 00 2a`. That is why a hex dump of x86 memory shows multi-byte numbers that look reversed.

blocks.caption: Each line of output checks one idea from this lesson: wraparound, two's complement, sign extension, byte order, and the floating point surprise below.

blocks.md: Fractions use a different encoding, **floating point**, standardized as IEEE 754 (a standard of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, IEEE). A C `double` is 64 bits: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits and 52 fraction bits, a binary form of scientific notation ($\pm 1.f \times 2^{e}$). Only fractions of the form $x / 2^k$ are exact. One tenth is not: in binary it repeats forever (0.000110011...), so 0.1 is stored rounded, and so is 0.2. Their rounded sum is the double just above the one nearest 0.3, which is why `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is false in C. This course needs no more floating point than that.
Bits have no type. The byte `0xf4` is 244, or -12, or part of a jump instruction, depending on which instruction reads it. Hex is a compact way to write bits: one digit for every 4 bits.

Misconception: "signed overflow wraps in C too." The hardware adder wraps, but in C, overflowing a signed integer is [undefined behavior](https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/language/operator_arithmetic), and compilers optimize on the assumption that it never happens. Only unsigned arithmetic is guaranteed to wrap modulo $2^n$.

blocks.question: What is `0x3c` in decimal?
blocks.explain: 3 x 16 + 12 = 60 (c is 12). In bits: 0011 1100 = 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 = 60. 36 comes from multiplying the digits, 3 x 12, and 312 from gluing the digits 3 and 12 together.

blocks.question: What range of values fits in a signed 8-bit integer (two's complement)?
blocks.explain: The top bit weighs -128, so the smallest value is 1000 0000 = -128 and the largest is 0111 1111 = 127. There is one more negative value than positive ones because 0 uses a pattern with the top bit clear. 0 to 255 is the unsigned range of the same 8 bits.

blocks.question: An `int` holding `0x12345678` is stored at address 0x100 on x86-64. Which byte is at address 0x100?
blocks.explain: x86-64 is little-endian: the least significant byte, 0x78, goes at the lowest address, followed by 0x56, 0x34 and 0x12 at 0x101 to 0x103. A big-endian machine would put 0x12 first.

lessons.title: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat

blocks.md: Inside the CPU, the state a program can see is small: a handful of **registers** and the **program counter**. A register is a tiny, very fast storage slot inside the CPU; x86-64 has 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers (`rax`, `rbx`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `rsi`, `rdi`, `rbp`, `rsp`, `r8` to `r15`). The program counter, called `rip` on x86-64 (the instruction pointer, with the r that marks 64-bit register names), holds the memory address of the next instruction.

The CPU then does one thing forever:

1. **Fetch** the instruction bytes at the address in the program counter.
2. **Decode** them: which operation, which registers or memory operands.
3. **Execute** it: compute, load from or store to memory, and update the program counter, either to the next instruction or to a jump target.

That is the whole model. Every loop, `if` and function call is built from it.

blocks.caption: A tiny function. We compile it with clang, a widely used C compiler, at its basic optimization level -O1 for x86-64 Linux and run it by hand.

blocks.md: Two conventions to read the trace. The assembly is in **AT&T syntax**: `addq %rcx, %rax` means "add rcx into rax" (source first, destination last). The name comes from AT&T, whose Unix assemblers used it; Intel's own manuals write the destination first. The last letter of an instruction name gives the operand size: `q` for quadword (64 bits) and `l` for long (32 bits), so `addq` is a 64-bit add, and `%ecx` names the low 32 bits of `rcx`. And the **System V x86-64 ABI** (application binary interface: the calling rules Linux uses, named after System V, the AT&T Unix release whose binary interface standard these rules extend) passes the first integer arguments in `rdi` and `rsi` and returns the result in `rax`. So `a` arrives in `rdi`, `n` in `rsi`, and the answer must end up in `rax`.

blocks.title: Stepping through sum(a, 3) instruction by instruction
blocks.code:
sum:
  testq %rsi, %rsi          # 0x00  is n <= 0?
  jle   .LBB0_1              # 0x03  if so, skip the loop
  xorl  %ecx, %ecx           # 0x05  i = 0
  xorl  %eax, %eax           # 0x07  s = 0
  nopl  0x0(%rax)            # 0x09  7 bytes of padding
.LBB0_4:
  addq  (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax  # 0x10  s += a[i]
  incq  %rcx                 # 0x14  i++
  cmpq  %rcx, %rsi           # 0x17  compare n with i
  jne   .LBB0_4              # 0x1a  loop if i != n
  retq                       # 0x1c  return s (in rax)
.LBB0_1:
  xorl  %eax, %eax           # 0x1d  return 0
  retq                       # 0x1f

scenes.caption: Called as sum(a, 3) with a at address 0x1000 holding 3, 1, 4. The ABI put a in rdi and n in rsi. testq sets the CPU's flags from n AND n, which is just n (zero? negative?), which the next jump, jle (jump if less or equal), reads; lesson 4 opens this up.
n is 3, so the conditional jump is not taken. The CPU simply moves on: rip advances past this 2-byte instruction to 0x05.

Two xorl instructions zero i (rcx) and s (rax). XOR (exclusive or: 1 where two bits differ) of a register with itself is 0; writing a 32-bit register also clears its upper 32 bits. nopl after them does nothing: it is padding so the loop starts at 0x10.
First trip through the loop. addq computes the address rdi + 8 x rcx = 0x1000, loads 3 from memory, and adds it to rax.
incq makes i = 1, cmpq compares n with i, and jne (jump if not equal) sees they differ, so it writes 0x10 into rip. That jump is the whole loop.
Second trip: address 0x1000 + 8 x 1 = 0x1008 holds 1, so s becomes 4.
Third trip: address 0x1010 holds 4, so s becomes 8.
Now i = 3 equals n, so jne is not taken and execution falls through to retq.
retq returns to the caller with the answer 8 in rax. In total the CPU executed 18 instructions: 5 before the loop, 4 per element, and 1 return.

blocks.md: Each line above is stored as bytes. Disassembling the object file with `objdump -d` shows them; instructions on x86-64 vary in length, so the program counter advances by a different amount each time.

blocks.code:
10: 48 03 04 cf     addq  (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax
  14: 48 ff c1        incq  %rcx
  17: 48 39 ce        cmpq  %rcx, %rsi
  1a: 75 f4           jne   0x10
  1c: c3              retq
blocks.caption: The loop body as machine code (offsets in hex). 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 bytes, then a 1-byte return.

blocks.prompt: The jump `jne` is encoded as just two bytes, `75 f4`. The byte `f4` is the signed number -12. Where does it send the CPU?
blocks.reveal: To **0x10**, the top of the loop. A jump offset is a signed byte in two's complement (lesson 2): f4 is 244 unsigned, and with its top bit set it means 244 - 256 = -12. By the time the jump executes, the program counter already points at the next instruction, 0x1c. A taken jump adds the offset: 0x1c - 12 = 0x10. There is no special loop hardware: a jump is just an instruction that writes a new value into the program counter.

blocks.md: Control flow is the program counter. Straight-line code advances it by the instruction length; `jmp`, conditional jumps, `call` and `ret` overwrite it. A C `for` loop compiles to a compare plus a conditional jump backwards.

Simplified: real CPUs pipeline and overlap many instructions, and even execute them out of order (lesson 7). But they are built so that the visible result is exactly as if each instruction ran one at a time in program order, which is why this model is the right one to reason with.

blocks.question: Using the same compiled code, how many instructions does the CPU execute for sum(a, 1000)?
blocks.explain: 5 instructions run once before the loop (test, jle, two xors, the padding nop), the 4-instruction loop body runs 1000 times, and retq runs once: 5 + 4000 + 1 = 4006. Instruction count grows with n because the loop body is re-fetched and re-executed each iteration.

blocks.question: In `addq (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax`, why is rcx multiplied by 8?
options: Because x86-64 has 8 general-purpose registers
Because the loop is unrolled 8 times
Because memory is read in 8-bit units
Because each long is 8 bytes, so element i starts 8 x i bytes after a
blocks.explain: Memory is addressed in bytes, and a long is 8 bytes on x86-64 Linux. a[i] therefore lives at address a + 8 x i. The CPU computes that address as part of the instruction (base rdi plus index rcx times scale 8).

lessons.title: Decisions in machine code: flags, compare and conditional jumps

blocks.md: Every `if`, `while` and `for` makes the CPU choose between two next instructions. Take `if (x > y)` with x = 7 and y = 3. x86-64 splits the decision into two instructions. A **compare** computes something from x and y and records facts about the result in the **condition flags**, single-bit registers inside the CPU. Then a **conditional jump** reads the flags and either writes a new address into the program counter or lets execution fall through to the next instruction. Lesson 3's trace used this pair twice (testq with jle, cmpq with jne) without opening it up.

Four flags matter, each named for what it reports about the last result:

- **ZF**, zero flag: the result was 0.
- **SF**, sign flag: the result's top bit is 1, so read as signed it is negative.
- **CF**, carry flag: the operation carried out of the top bit, or for a subtraction borrowed into it. After a - b, CF = 1 means a < b as unsigned numbers.
- **OF**, overflow flag: the signed result did not fit, as when two positive numbers add up to a negative one.

`cmp b, a` (AT&T order) computes a - b, sets the flags as a subtraction would, and throws the difference away. `test b, a` does the same with bitwise AND (each result bit is 1 only where both inputs have a 1): `testq %rsi, %rsi` asked whether n was zero (ZF) or negative (SF). The size suffix b, as in `cmpb` below, means a 1-byte operand, as q means 8 bytes and l 4.

blocks.title: Flags set by cmpb for five pairs of bytes

scenes.caption: 5 - 3 = 2: no flag is set. Read signed or unsigned, a is greater than b.
3 - 5 needs a borrow, so CF = 1: 3 is below 5 as unsigned. The result 0xfe has its top bit set, so SF = 1: negative as signed.
Equal values subtract to 0, so ZF = 1. je (jump if equal) reads exactly this flag.
0xff is 255 unsigned or -1 signed. 255 - 1 needs no borrow, CF = 0: above. But SF = 1, since -1 - 1 = -2: less. The same bits give opposite answers.
-128 - 1 = -129 does not fit in a byte; it wraps to 0x7f (+127) and OF = 1. SF alone would say greater, which is why signed less-than is defined as SF differing from OF.

blocks.md:
Conditional jumps test combinations of flags. The letters name the kind of comparison: **g**reater and **l**ess for signed numbers, **a**bove and **b**elow for unsigned ones.

- `je` / `jne` (equal, not equal): ZF = 1 / ZF = 0.
- `jl` (less, signed): SF differs from OF. `jge`: SF equals OF.
- `jg` (greater, signed): SF equals OF and ZF = 0. `jle`: SF differs from OF, or ZF = 1.
- `jb` (below, unsigned): CF = 1. `jae`, also written `jnb` (not below): CF = 0.
- `ja` (above, unsigned): CF = 0 and ZF = 0. `jbe`: CF = 1 or ZF = 1.

The compiler picks the signed or unsigned family from the C types of the values being compared.

blocks.caption: The two C functions differ only in their types. GCC chose jle for int and jnb for unsigned; it also wrote the unsigned compare with the operands swapped, which is just as correct.

blocks.prompt: Call both with x = -1 and y = 1 (for max_u, the -1 converts to the unsigned value `0xffffffff`). Which value does each function return?
blocks.reveal:
`max_s` returns **1**, since -1 < 1. `max_u` returns **4294967295**: the same 32 bits read as unsigned are the largest 32-bit value, which is greater than 1. Real output from the same compiler:

```
max_s(7, 3)  = 7
max_s(-1, 1) = 1
max_u(-1, 1) = 4294967295
```

The trace below shows which flags made each decision.

blocks.title: Signed and unsigned max, both outcomes
blocks.code:
max_s:                 # int max_s(int x, int y)
  movl  %esi, %eax     # result = y
  cmpl  %esi, %edi     # flags from x - y
  jle   .L2            # signed: x <= y? keep y
  movl  %edi, %eax     # result = x
.L2:
  ret
max_u:                 # unsigned max_u(unsigned x, unsigned y)
  movl  %esi, %eax     # result = y
  cmpl  %edi, %esi     # flags from y - x
  jnb   .L4            # unsigned: y >= x? keep y
  movl  %edi, %eax     # result = x
.L4:
  ret

scenes.caption: max_s(7, 3). result starts as y = 3, then cmpl computes x - y = 7 - 3 = 4 and sets the flags: none of them, since 4 is positive, nonzero and fits.
jle jumps if SF differs from OF or ZF = 1. Both are false, so the jump is not taken and execution falls through to the next line.
movl copies x into the result and ret returns 7.
max_s(-1, 1). x is 0xffffffff. cmpl computes -1 - 1 = -2 = 0xfffffffe: SF = 1, and no signed overflow, so OF = 0.
SF differs from OF, so jle is taken: the program counter jumps to .L2 and ret returns y = 1. Signed, -1 is less than 1.
max_u(0xffffffff, 1). GCC compares the other way round here: cmpl computes y - x = 1 - 4294967295, which borrows, so CF = 1. The 32-bit result is 2.
jnb (jump if not below) jumps only when CF = 0. CF is 1, meaning y is below x, so it falls through: result = x, and ret returns 4294967295.

blocks.md: A loop is a conditional jump that goes backwards. GCC at -Og compiles `while (s[n] != 0) n++;` (the heart of `strlen`) with the test at the bottom: one unconditional `jmp` goes straight to the test, and the test jumps back to the body for as long as the byte is not 0. For the string "hi", `cmpb` runs 3 times (for h, i and the final 0 byte) and `jne` is taken twice.

blocks.caption: The loop body is one instruction; the compare and the backward jump are the loop.

blocks.md:
Jumps are not the only way to act on flags. At -O1 GCC compiles both max functions with no jump at all:

```
max_s:  cmpl %esi, %edi
        movl %esi, %eax
        cmovge %edi, %eax
        ret
```

`cmovge` is a **conditional move**: it copies x into the result only if the flags say greater or equal, and otherwise does nothing (`max_u` gets `cmovnb`). Both candidate values already sit in registers, so there is nothing to jump over. Compilers use conditional moves only when computing both sides is safe and cheap; lesson 7 shows why avoiding a jump can make code faster.

An `if` is a compare that sets flags plus a conditional jump that reads them. Signed and unsigned comparisons differ only in which flags the jump reads: SF and OF for signed (jl, jg), CF for unsigned (jb, ja).
Misconception: "the CPU knows whether a value is signed." It does not. `cmp` sets all four flags every time; the signedness lives only in which jump the compiler chose after it.

blocks.question: `cmpb` compares a = 0x80 with b = 0x01, setting the flags from a - b. Which of the jumps `jl` (signed less) and `ja` (unsigned above) would be taken?
options: Both: signed, -128 is less than 1; unsigned, 128 is above 1
Only jl
Only ja
Neither, because the subtraction overflowed
blocks.explain: The result 0x7f sets OF = 1 and SF = 0, so SF differs from OF and jl is taken: -128 < 1. No borrow happened (CF = 0) and the result is not zero (ZF = 0), so ja is taken too: 128 > 1. One compare answers both questions; the jump picks which.

blocks.question: In C, `int len = -1; unsigned size = 10;` and then `if (len < size) ...`. What happens?
options: The condition is true, because -1 is less than 10
It does not compile
The condition is false: len is converted to unsigned (4294967295) and the compiler emits an unsigned comparison
The CPU raises an overflow exception
blocks.explain: When an int meets an unsigned in a comparison, C converts the int to unsigned. -1 becomes 0xffffffff = 4294967295, and the compiler uses an unsigned jump (from the below/above family). 4294967295 < 10 is false. Compilers warn about this with -Wsign-compare.

lessons.title: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack

blocks.md: Every process gets an **address space**: the range of memory addresses it can use, which looks to the program like one long array of bytes. The OSTEP textbook's model divides it into three parts. The **code** (the program's instructions) and static data (global variables) sit at fixed places. The **heap** holds memory requested at run time with `malloc` and released with `free`. The **stack** holds local variables, saved registers and return addresses for function calls. Each call gets its own chunk of the stack, its **stack frame**, which is freed when the call returns.

scenes.caption: Code and static data come straight from the executable file; their size is known before the program starts.
The heap grows toward higher addresses as malloc asks the OS for more memory. Heap memory lives until free is called.
The stack starts high and grows toward lower addresses with each call. A frame disappears as soon as its function returns.
Simplified: real layouts also include shared libraries, memory-mapped files and randomized start addresses. The big gap lets both heap and stack grow.

blocks.md:
The stack is managed with one register, `rsp`, the **stack pointer**, which holds the address of the top of the stack. On x86-64 the stack grows toward lower addresses: `push` subtracts 8 from `rsp` and stores a value there; `pop` loads it and adds 8 back. A function call is just two instructions: `call f` pushes the **return address** (the address of the instruction after the call) and jumps to `f`; `ret` pops that address into the program counter.

The ABI adds one rule: `rsp` must be a multiple of 16 whenever a `call` executes, so instructions that move 16 bytes at once find aligned stack slots. Because `call` itself pushes 8 bytes, every function starts 8 bytes off that boundary, and each push moves it another 8. In `sumsq` below, two register saves keep it 8 off, so one extra 8-byte push restores alignment before it calls `square`.

blocks.code:
__attribute__((noinline)) long square(long x) { return x * x; }
long sumsq(long a, long b) { return square(a) + square(b); }

# clang -O1, x86-64 Linux
square:                    sumsq:
  movq  %rdi, %rax           pushq %r14
  imulq %rdi, %rax           pushq %rbx
  retq                       pushq %rax       # 8 bytes of padding
                             movq  %rsi, %rbx
                             callq square
                             movq  %rax, %r14
                             movq  %rbx, %rdi
                             callq square
                             addq  %r14, %rax
                             addq  $8, %rsp   # drop the padding
                             popq  %rbx
                             popq  %r14
                             retq
blocks.caption: Real compiler output. noinline stops clang from merging square into sumsq so we can watch the calls.

scenes.caption: main has just executed call sumsq. The call pushed the return address into main (ret:m), so rsp = S. Arguments arrived in registers: rdi = 3, rsi = 4.
sumsq saves r14 and rbx, which the ABI says a function must preserve for its caller, then pushes rax only as 8 bytes of padding so rsp is a multiple of 16 at the next call, as the ABI requires.
b = 4 is copied into rbx, then call square pushes the return address into sumsq (ret:s) and jumps. rsp = S-32.
square computes 3 x 3 = 9 in rax and executes ret, which pops ret:s into the program counter. Back in sumsq, 9 is stashed in r14.
The second call reuses the very same slot: push ret:s, square(4) returns 16, pop. addq then makes rax = 9 + 16 = 25.
sumsq drops the padding, restores rbx and r14, and ret pops ret:m. The stack is exactly as main left it, and the result 25 is in rax.

blocks.prompt: A buggy function copies 40 bytes of user input into a 16-byte local array on the stack. What can go wrong when the function executes `ret`?
blocks.reveal: The extra bytes overwrite whatever lies above the array in the frame, which can include saved registers and the **return address**. `ret` blindly pops that slot into the program counter, so the CPU jumps wherever the input bytes say: usually a crash, and in the classic **stack buffer overflow** attack, code of the attacker's choosing. The CPU has no idea the value was not written by `call`.

blocks.md: `call` = push return address + jump. `ret` = pop into the program counter. Everything a function keeps on the stack lives only until it returns, which is why the stack can be reused so cheaply.

Never return a pointer to a local variable. Its stack slot is reused by the very next call (as the second call to square reused the first one's slot), so the pointer soon points at unrelated data. Use the heap (malloc) for data that must outlive the function.

blocks.question: Why does sumsq copy b into rbx before calling square, instead of leaving it in rsi?
options: Because rsi is reserved for return values
Because square may overwrite rsi freely, while the ABI requires square to preserve rbx
Because rbx is faster than rsi
Because the stack is full
blocks.explain: The System V ABI splits registers into caller-saved ones (like rdi, rsi, rax) that any callee may clobber, and callee-saved ones (rbx, rbp, r12 to r15) that a callee must restore before returning. That is also why sumsq itself pushes rbx and r14 first: it is about to use them and must hand them back intact.

blocks.question: Right after `call square` executes, which statement is true?
options: rsp increased by 8 and the program counter points at square
rsp is unchanged; the return address is kept in a special register
rsp decreased by 8, the stack top holds the address of the instruction after the call, and the program counter points at square
rsp decreased by 8 and the stack top holds the address of square
blocks.explain: The stack grows down, so a push subtracts 8 from rsp. call pushes the return address (the next instruction in the caller), not the target, then jumps by writing square's address into the program counter.

lessons.title: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it

blocks.md: So far each `addq` that read memory looked as cheap as one that only touched registers. It is not. Main memory (DRAM, dynamic random-access memory: any address can be read in about the same time) sits off the CPU chip and takes far longer to answer than the CPU takes to execute an instruction. DRAM is called dynamic because each bit is a tiny capacitor whose charge leaks away and must be refreshed over and over. Time here is counted in **cycles**, ticks of the CPU's clock: at 3 GHz one cycle lasts a third of a nanosecond. To hide that gap, CPUs keep copies of recently used memory in small, fast on-chip memories called **caches**, organized in levels: L1 is smallest and fastest, then L2, and often L3. When the data an access needs is already in a cache, that is a **hit**; when it is not and must be fetched from further away, that is a **miss**.

blocks.title: Cost of one access, in CPU cycles (Intel Pentium M)

scenes.caption: Ulrich Drepper's memory paper lists Intel's numbers for the Pentium M, a 2003 laptop chip: about 3 cycles for L1d (the level 1 data cache), 14 for L2, 240 for main memory. Newer CPUs differ, but the gap of roughly two orders of magnitude remains.
One trip to main memory costs as much time as 80 L1 hits (240 / 3 = 80). A program that misses the cache often spends most of its time waiting, not computing.

blocks.md: Caches do not store single bytes. They move fixed-size blocks called **cache lines**, and as Ulrich Drepper (a Red Hat engineer, then glibc's maintainer) notes in his 2007 paper, 64 bytes is now the norm. A miss on one byte brings in its 63 neighbours too. This works because programs show **locality** (OSTEP's terms): **temporal** locality (data used recently is likely used again soon, like a loop counter) and **spatial** locality (data near a recent access is likely next, like the next array element).

C stores a 2D array in **row-major** order: `a[i][j]` and `a[i][j+1]` are neighbours, while `a[i+1][j]` is a whole row away. Take a tiny 4 by 8 array of 8-byte longs, so each row fills exactly one 64-byte line, and a toy cache that holds only 2 lines and evicts the least recently used one (LRU). Summing it row by row and column by column does the same additions, but not the same memory traffic.

Two terms for the larger example that follows. A kibibyte is 2^10 = 1024 bytes and a mebibyte is 2^20 bytes, written KiB and MiB. A **fully associative** cache lets any line sit in any of its slots, the simplest kind to reason about.

blocks.title: Hits and misses: row order vs column order

scenes.caption: Row-by-row order. The first access a[0][0] misses: the cache fetches the whole 64-byte line, which is all 8 longs of row 0.
The other 7 elements of row 0 are already in that line: 7 hits. This is spatial locality paying off.
After the whole array: 4 misses and 28 hits. One miss per line, no matter how small the cache.
Column-by-column order with the same 2-line cache. a[0][0], a[1][0], a[2][0], a[3][0] are in 4 different lines: 4 misses, and the first two lines are already evicted.
Moving to column 1, a[0][1] needs row 0's line again, but it was evicted. Every access misses.
After the whole array: 32 misses out of 32. Same data, same additions, 8x the misses, purely from access order.

blocks.prompt: Scale up: a 1024 by 1024 array of longs (8 MiB) and a 32 KiB cache (512 lines, fully associative, LRU). What fraction of accesses miss when summing row by row, and column by column?
blocks.reveal: Simulated: row order misses **12.5%** (one miss per 8 longs), column order misses **100%**. The sizes: 1024 x 1024 longs × 8 bytes = 8 MiB, and the cache holds 32 KiB / 64 bytes = 512 lines. Column order jumps a whole row, 1024 x 8 bytes = 8 KiB, between accesses, so each one lands in a new line, and by the time the loop returns to a line, 1023 other lines have pushed it out of the 512-line cache.

blocks.tex: \text{average access time} = t_{\text{hit}} + (\text{miss rate}) \times t_{\text{miss penalty}}
blocks.caption: A simple one-level cache model: every access pays the hit time, and misses also pay the trip to memory.

blocks.md: Plug in the Pentium M numbers ($t_\text{hit} = 3$, penalty $= 240$ cycles). Row order: $3 + 0.125 \times 240 = 33$ cycles per access. Column order: $3 + 1 \times 240 = 243$ cycles, about 7.4x slower for identical arithmetic.

blocks.title: Average access time vs miss rate

scenes.caption: With a 240-cycle penalty, the line is steep: every extra percent of misses adds 2.4 cycles to the average access.
If misses only go to L2 (Drepper's L2 takes about 14 cycles, so roughly 11 more than an L1 hit), even a high miss rate is tolerable. The two points still mark the 240-cycle case.

blocks.md: Simplified model. Real CPUs have several cache levels, and **hardware prefetchers** detect sequential and strided access (every k-th element, a fixed step apart) and fetch lines before they are asked for, hiding much of the cost of row order (and some of column order). Measured slowdowns vary by machine; the direction does not.
Performance is often decided by memory access patterns, not instruction counts. Touch memory sequentially, reuse data while it is still in cache, and keep hot data small.

blocks.question: A colleague's loop `for j: for i: total += m[i][j]` over a large C 2D array of longs is slow. What is the most effective first fix?
options: Swap the loops so the inner loop walks j along a row
Use a faster add instruction
Make total a global variable
Add more threads before changing anything
blocks.explain: In C, m[i][j] and m[i][j+1] are adjacent, so walking j in the inner loop uses all 8 longs of every 64-byte line it fetches. The current inner loop strides a full row per access, fetching a new line every time.

blocks.question: With a 3-cycle hit time and a 240-cycle miss penalty, what is the average access time at a 5% miss rate?
options: 12 cycles
15 cycles
243 cycles
8 cycles
blocks.explain: 3 + 0.05 x 240 = 3 + 12 = 15 cycles. Note that a 5% miss rate already makes the average access 5x slower than a hit: misses dominate.

lessons.title: Why real CPUs beat the simple loop: pipelines and prediction

blocks.md: Lesson 3 ran instructions strictly one after another. Real CPUs overlap them, the way a laundry with a washer and a dryer does: while one load dries, the next one washes. A **pipeline** splits the work of one instruction into **stages**, and in every clock cycle each stage works on a different instruction. The classic teaching design has five stages: **fetch** the instruction, **decode** it and read its registers, **execute** the arithmetic, access **memory** for loads and stores, and **write back** the result into a register.

blocks.title: Five instructions with and without a pipeline

scenes.caption: Without a pipeline, instruction I1 passes through all five stages, one per clock cycle, while the other four stages sit idle.
Only then does I2 start. Five instructions take 5 x 5 = 25 cycles, and each stage is busy just one cycle in five.
Pipelined: I2 is fetched while I1 is decoded, and so on. The same five instructions finish after 9 cycles.
In cycle 5 every stage holds a different instruction: I5 is being fetched while I1 writes back. From here on, one instruction finishes per cycle.

blocks.caption: Cycles for n instructions on k stages with no stalls. k = 5, n = 5: 9 vs 25. For n = 1000: 1004 vs 5000, close to one instruction per cycle.

blocks.md: A pipeline does not make any single instruction faster: each still passes through all five stages, so its **latency** stays 5 cycles. It raises **throughput**, the rate at which instructions finish. The flow breaks on **hazards**. A **data hazard** arises when an instruction needs a result that an earlier one has not written back yet, like each `addq` in the sum loop needing the previous value of `rax`. The simple fix is to **stall**: hold the instruction back a cycle or two, leaving an empty slot called a bubble. The better fix is **forwarding** (also called bypassing): extra wiring that hands a result from the end of execute straight to the next instruction's execute, without waiting for write-back.

A **control hazard** comes from jumps. Fetch must pick the next address every cycle, but a conditional jump only knows whether it is taken once it reaches execute. Rather than wait, the CPU uses **branch prediction**: it guesses the direction from what this jump did on earlier runs, and keeps fetching down the guessed path. Work done on a guess is **speculative**: its results are held back until the jump is resolved. A wrong guess is a **misprediction**: the pipeline is flushed, the speculative work is discarded, and fetch restarts at the right address.

blocks.title: A mispredicted jump in a five-stage pipeline

scenes.caption: The conditional jump jne is fetched in cycle 1. Whether it is taken is known only after execute, so the predictor guesses and fetch carries on down the guessed path.
Execute finds the guess was wrong. The two guessed instructions have changed nothing visible yet, so they are simply flushed, and fetch restarts at the right address.
The right instruction finishes in cycle 8 instead of cycle 6: 2 cycles lost, one per stage that held wrong work. Simplified: real cores resolve jumps 15 or more stages deep and lose that many cycles.

blocks.md: Agner Fog, who measures these effects on real chips, notes that a misprediction wastes roughly as many cycles as the pipeline is long. Modern cores have far more than five stages: the penalties Fog measured are 15 to 20 cycles on Intel's Haswell to Skylake family and about 18 on AMD Zen 1 to 3. Predictors are very good at regular patterns, such as a loop jump that is taken 999 times and falls through once. No predictor can guess a branch that depends on random data.

blocks.prompt: A loop adds up only the array elements that are at least 128, using an `if`. The array holds a million random values from 0 to 255. Will the loop run faster if the array is sorted first, even though it does exactly the same additions?
blocks.reveal: **Yes, several times faster** when the compiler keeps the `if` as a jump. With random data the jump goes each way about half the time with no pattern, so the predictor is wrong about half the time and pays the penalty on each miss. Sorted, the jump goes one way for the whole first half and the other way for the whole second half, so the predictor is almost always right. The measurement below shows it.

blocks.caption: The threshold loop with a timer. noinline and the empty asm statement stop the compiler from merging or skipping the 20 repeats.

blocks.code:
# gcc 13.2 -O1 -fno-if-conversion: keeps the if as a jump
random order: 4.09 ns per element
sorted order: 0.44 ns per element

# gcc 13.2 -O1: GCC turns the if into cmovg
random order: 0.66 ns per element
sorted order: 0.67 ns per element
blocks.caption: Real runs on Compiler Explorer's x86-64 runners, shared cloud machines (the runs above on an Intel Xeon Platinum 8375C), so timings are noisy. Over four runs each: with the jump, random 4.1 to 6.2 ns and sorted 0.4 to 1.3 ns; with cmov, 0.7 to 1.1 ns in either order.

blocks.title: Toy model: cycles per element of the threshold loop

scenes.caption: Toy model, not a measurement: 2 cycles of work per element, a 17-cycle misprediction penalty (inside Agner Fog's 15 to 20), and half the random elements mispredicted: 2 + 0.5 x 17 = 10.5. cmov always pays 3.
The same model with the 2-cycle penalty of the five-stage pipeline above: 2 + 0.5 x 2 = 3. Short pipelines barely care about prediction; deep modern ones care a lot.

blocks.md: The conditional move from lesson 4 avoids the problem entirely. At plain -O1, GCC turned the `if` into `cmovg`, so there is no jump to predict, and sorted or random order makes no real difference. It is not always better: a well-predicted jump lets the CPU skip the work of the side not taken, while a conditional move always computes both. Compilers weigh that case by case, which is why the same source can behave so differently at different settings.

Pipelines are only the start. Modern x86-64 cores split instructions into simpler **micro-operations** and execute them **out of order**: when one is waiting for data, say a load that missed the cache (lesson 6), later ones whose inputs are ready run first. Results are then **retired** in program order, so registers and memory change exactly as if the instructions ran one at a time, the promise lesson 3 relied on. Independent instructions can overlap; a **dependency chain**, where each instruction needs the previous result, cannot. Finally, a chip usually has several **cores**: each is a complete CPU with its own registers and program counter, running its own instruction stream, and all of them share the same memory.

Pipelining raises throughput, not the speed of any single instruction. The flow breaks on dependencies on recent results and on jumps the predictor gets wrong; a misprediction costs roughly the pipeline's length in cycles.

Misconception: "fewer instructions always means faster code." The two versions of the threshold loop do about the same work per element, yet one ran several times slower on random data. Predictability of branches, like the memory access pattern in lesson 6, can matter more than the instruction count.

blocks.question: An ideal five-stage pipeline (no stalls, no mispredictions) runs 100 instructions. How many cycles does it take?
blocks.explain: The first instruction needs 5 cycles to get through all five stages, and after that one more instruction finishes every cycle: 5 + 99 = 104. 500 is the unpipelined time; exactly 100 would ignore the cycles needed to fill the pipeline.

blocks.question: A profile shows a hot loop whose `if` on input data is mispredicted about half the time. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Add a few more instructions before the if so the CPU has time to think
Make the outcome predictable or branch-free, for example sort or group the data, or let the compiler use a conditional move
Split the loop across two functions
Turn off out-of-order execution
blocks.explain: The cost comes from flushing the pipeline on each wrong guess. Removing the guess (a conditional move) or making it right almost every time (sorted or grouped data) removes the penalty. Extra instructions or function boundaries do not make the direction any easier to predict.

lessons.title: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU

blocks.md: Two problems remain. A program must not be able to read another program's files or drive the disk directly, yet it needs to do I/O. And one program must not be able to hog the CPU forever. The OSTEP textbook calls the solution **limited direct execution**: the program runs directly on the CPU at full speed, but in a restricted processor mode.

The CPU has at least two modes. In **user mode**, privileged operations such as issuing I/O or reconfiguring the hardware are refused: attempting one raises an exception and the OS takes over. In **kernel mode**, where the OS runs, everything is allowed. A program asks the OS for a service with a **system call**: a special **trap** instruction that switches to kernel mode and jumps to a handler the kernel registered at boot in a **trap table**. A **return-from-trap** instruction later drops back to user mode.

On x86-64 Linux, the `syscall(2)` man page (section 2 of the manual documents system calls) gives the exact rules: the trap instruction is `syscall`, the system call number goes in `rax`, arguments go in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `r10`, `r8`, `r9`, and the result comes back in `rax`. The kernel's table lists `write` as number 1. So `printf` eventually becomes a `write(1, buf, len)` call, where 1 is standard output.

scenes.caption: An ordinary function call into the C library's write wrapper. Still user mode, no OS involved yet.
The wrapper puts 1 (the number for write) in rax and the arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, then executes the syscall instruction. The CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to the kernel's entry point.
The kernel checks that file descriptor 1 is open and that buf is memory this process may read, then hands the 3 bytes to the terminal's driver, the kernel code that operates that device.
Return-from-trap: back to user mode with the result, 3 bytes written, in rax. The wrapper returns it as an ordinary function result.

blocks.md: System calls give the OS control when a program asks. But what if it never asks, say it is stuck in `while (1) {}`? The answer, per OSTEP, is a **timer interrupt**: a hardware timer is programmed to interrupt the CPU every so many milliseconds. Each interrupt forcibly runs an OS handler, so the OS regains control no matter what the program does.

Once in control, the OS **scheduler** may decide to run a different process. It performs a **context switch**: it saves the current process's registers, including the program counter and stack pointer, into that process's kernel data, then restores another process's saved registers. When the return-from-trap executes, the CPU resumes the other process exactly where it was interrupted.

scenes.caption: Simplified model: each process gets a 10 ms time slice, after which the timer interrupts, and kernel work takes 1 ms (exaggerated so it is visible). Process A runs on the CPU directly, in user mode.
The timer interrupt fires. The kernel saves A's registers and restores B's: a context switch.
B runs until the next timer interrupt, then the kernel switches back. A resumes at the exact instruction it was on and cannot tell it was paused.
At 27 ms A calls read() on a file whose data must come from disk. A cannot continue until it arrives, so the kernel marks A blocked and runs B instead of letting the CPU sit idle.

blocks.prompt: A process runs `while (1) {}` and never makes a system call. On a single-core machine (one core: one CPU that runs one instruction stream at a time), can it freeze everything else?
blocks.reveal: No. The timer interrupt fires regardless of what user code is doing, the kernel's handler runs, and the scheduler can switch to other processes. The loop only burns its own time slices. And the process cannot turn the timer off: reprogramming it is a privileged operation, refused in user mode.

blocks.md: The OS is not running alongside your program; it runs only when something hands it the CPU: a system call (the program asks), an exception (the program did something illegal), or an interrupt (hardware such as the timer or the disk demands attention).

blocks.question: Which of these operations has to go through a system call?
options: Reading bytes from a file
Adding two numbers in registers
Calling a function defined in your own program
Writing to a local variable on the stack
blocks.explain: Arithmetic, function calls and stack accesses are ordinary user-mode instructions on the process's own memory. A file lives on a device that only the kernel may touch, so read() must trap into the kernel.

blocks.question: Why does a system call use a trap instruction instead of letting the program jump directly to the kernel's code for write?
options: Jumps cannot reach addresses that large
Trap instructions are faster than jumps
The trap switches to kernel mode and enters only at handlers the kernel registered, so a program cannot run arbitrary kernel code with full privileges
The C library has no way to call functions
blocks.explain: If user code could jump anywhere into the kernel with privileges, it could skip permission checks. The trap table, set up at boot in kernel mode, fixes the only entry points, and the mode switch happens in hardware as part of the trap.

lessons.title: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses

blocks.md: Two processes can use the very same address, say for a global variable, and still each hold a different value there. That works because addresses a program uses are **virtual**. On every memory access, hardware in the CPU, the **memory management unit** (MMU), translates the virtual address into a **physical** address in RAM, using a table the OS maintains separately for each process.

With **paging**, memory is cut into fixed-size **pages** (virtual) and **frames** (physical) of the same size. A virtual address splits into a **virtual page number** (VPN), its high bits, and an **offset** within the page, its low bits. The per-process **page table** maps each VPN to a physical frame number (PFN). The offset is not translated: it only says which byte within the page.

The OSTEP textbook's tiny example: a 64-byte address space with 16-byte pages, so 4 pages, a 2-bit VPN and a 4-bit offset. The bit counts follow from the sizes: 64 = 2^6, so an address has 6 bits; 16 = 2^4, so the low 4 bits pick the byte within a page; the 2 bits left over number the 4 pages. Its page table maps virtual page 0 to frame 3, page 1 to frame 7, page 2 to frame 5 and page 3 to frame 2. The program loads from virtual address 21.

scenes.caption: 21 in binary is 010101. Nothing is translated yet.
16-byte pages need 4 offset bits (2^4 = 16), leaving the top 2 bits as the VPN: 01, virtual page 1. The offset 0101 is byte 5 within that page.
The MMU indexes the page table with VPN 1 and finds physical frame 7.
Replace the VPN with the PFN, keep the offset: 111 then 0101 gives 1110101, physical address 117. The load reads RAM byte 117.

blocks.md: Real x86-64 numbers. Pages are 4 KiB, so the offset is 12 bits ($2^{12} = 4096$). With 4-level paging, still the default for ordinary programs (newer server CPUs add a fifth level for 57-bit addresses), virtual addresses use 48 bits; Linux's documented memory map gives user space the lower half, 128 TB: 2^47 bytes, half of the 2^48 that 48 bits can name (here TB means 2^40 bytes). A single flat table for the remaining 36 bits (48 minus the 12 offset bits) would be huge, so the page table is a tree of 4 levels. Each table node is one 4 KiB page of 8-byte entries, which is 4096 / 8 = 512 entries; 512 = 2^9, so each level consumes 9 bits: $4 \times 9 + 12 = 48$.

scenes.caption: A typical user-space stack address. The low 48 bits are split into four 9-bit table indices and a 12-bit offset.
Computed with shifts and masks (worked below): indices 255, 500, 145, 325. Each picks one of 512 entries in a table, whose entry points to the next level's table.
The last-level entry gives the physical frame; the offset 0x678 (byte 1656) is copied through unchanged. A full walk costs up to 4 extra memory reads.

blocks.md: How one index is computed. Written in binary, the 48-bit address `0x7ffd12345678` begins `011111111 111110100 ...` (each hex digit is 4 bits, lesson 2). The top-level index is bits 47 to 39, found with two bit operations: `(addr >> 39) & 0x1ff`. The **right shift** `>> 39` slides every bit 39 places to the right and drops the 39 low bits off the end, leaving only the top 9 bits, `011111111`. The **AND** with the **mask** `0x1ff` (binary 1 1111 1111, nine ones) keeps the low 9 bits and zeroes the rest; here nothing above them remains, so the index is 0 1111 1111 = 255. The next level is `(addr >> 30) & 0x1ff`: the mask now cuts away bits 47 to 39, leaving `111110100` = 500.

Four extra memory reads per access would be ruinous, given lesson 6. So the MMU caches recent translations in a **translation lookaside buffer** (TLB), which OSTEP describes as a hardware cache of popular virtual-to-physical translations. Thanks to locality, most accesses hit in the TLB and skip the walk entirely. Page-table entries also carry a **present bit**: if a page is not in memory, the access raises a **page fault**, the OS runs, loads or allocates the page, and the instruction is retried. That is how the lazy loading from lesson 1 works.

blocks.prompt: Process A and process B both store a value at virtual address 0x7ffd12345678. Does B overwrite A's value?
blocks.reveal: No. Each process has its own page table, so the same virtual page maps to different physical frames. Neither process can even name the other's memory, since every address it can produce goes through its own table. This isolation is the foundation of process protection, and the OS switches page tables as part of every context switch between processes.

blocks.md: Every address your program uses is virtual. The MMU translates it on every access using the current process's page table, the TLB makes that fast, and page faults let the OS fill in memory lazily.

blocks.question: With 4 KiB pages, what is the offset within its page of virtual address 0x7ffd12345678?
blocks.explain: 4 KiB = 2^12 bytes, so the offset is the low 12 bits, which is the last 3 hex digits: 0x678. The remaining bits select the page through the 4-level table.

blocks.question: Why does x86-64 use a 4-level tree instead of one flat table indexed by the 36-bit page number?
options: A flat table cannot be cached in the TLB
Flat tables cannot hold physical frame numbers
Hardware cannot index arrays larger than 512 entries
A flat table would need 2^36 entries x 8 bytes = 512 GiB per process, mostly describing unused memory
blocks.explain: 2^36 x 8 bytes = 512 GiB (a gibibyte is 2^30 bytes), for every process. A tree only allocates the lower-level tables for regions actually in use, so a small process needs a few pages of page tables. The cost is the longer walk, which the TLB hides.
